# README.md

Source: https://github.com/mercuryworkshop/dreamlandjs/blob/rewrite/README.md

<h1 align="center">dreamland.js</h1>
<p align="center"><img src="./assets/logo.png" alt="logo" height="100"></p>

dreamland is a utilitarian JSX-based web framework with **no virtual dom** and **no build step**. It is less than 4kb minified + brotli'd (smaller than preact), gradually integrates with existing plain JS projects, and is reasonably easy to learn.

<div align="center">
 <a href="https://dreamland.js.org/docs/getting-started">Get Started</a> | <a href="https://dreamland.js.org">Documentation</a> | <a href="https://dreamland.js.org/playground">Playground</a> | <a href="https://discord.gg/GKKF3CmHPA">Discord</a>
</div>
<br/>

<div align="center">
  <img src="https://img.shields.io/github/issues/MercuryWorkshop/dreamlandjs?style=for-the-badge&color=purple" height="25"/>
  <img src="https://img.shields.io/github/stars/MercuryWorkshop/dreamlandjs?style=for-the-badge&color=purple" height="25"/>
</div>

Check out the [website](https://dreamland.js.org/docs/getting-started) to get started with dreamland. You can also try dreamland online in the [playground](https://dreamland.js.org/playground), which has dreamland and typescript set up already.

## Acknowledgements

dreamland uses the [parsel](https://github.com/LeaVerou/parsel) CSS selector parsing library to transform CSS in components.

---

# router.mdx

Source: https://github.com/mercuryworkshop/dreamlandjs/blob/rewrite/site/src/docs/extras/router.mdx

- Features
  - Router
order: 30

dreamland has a first-party react-router equivalent that supports most of the features react-router has.
It's designed to be a singleton component that is controlled via the `router` export in `dreamland/router`.
The router is constructed as a JSX component and routes are defined in JSX:

```tsx
<div id="app">
	<Router>
		<Route show={<MainPage />} />
		<Route layout={DocsLayout} path="docs">
			{docs.map(({ path, component }) => {
				return <Route path={path} show={() => jsx(component, {})} />;
			})}
		</Route>
	</Router>
</div>
```

Once a `Router` component is created, the instance is exposed by the `router` export.
The `Router` automatically handles the `popstate` event for history navigation.
It also exposes a `navigate` function to change the current route and commit it to history:

```tsx
import { router } from "dreamland/router";

router.navigate("/"); // sent to history
```

## Advanced route usage

### Dynamic routes

Route path segments with `:<name>` creates a dynamic prop for that path segment, and `*` consumes all further path segments and puts them in the `*` prop.
All `show` targets get a prop `routerParams`, an object that has any props from the path segment.

You can't rely on it always existing since the router does not construct the `show` target internally with the `routerParams` prop passed in.
Instead, the `routerParams` prop is assigned to the component state during routing.

### Layouts

Layouts are special components that get more information about routing and wrap children routes.
The router constructs the layout component internally, passing the `routerState` prop.

## Async routes (Suspense)

The router also supports `show` props that are functions that return promises, allowing for code splitting and lazy loading.
The component returned is cached and not reinstantiated.

By default, routing does not show any feedback while waiting for async routes to finish.
However, layouts can use `routerParams` to show a loading bar or placeholder.

### Corking
"Corked" routes are routes with a layout that are only fully instantiated on the client and eagerly switch to their layout when navigating in from other pages.
This allows for clientside only routes for browser-only things like Monaco.

Make a route with a layout corked using the `cork={true}` prop.

## SSR integration

dreamland's router is compatible with SSR and hydration. By default, it'll attempt to route to `[location.pathname, location.origin]` which won't work in SSR environment,
but this can be overridden with the `initial` prop:

```tsx
import { render } from "dreamland/ssr/server";

function App(this: FC<{ url?: string }>) {
	return (
		<div id="app">
			<Router initial={this.url ? [this.url, "http://127.0.0.1:5173"] : []}>
				{/* ... */}
			</Router>
		</div>
	)
}

export default (path) => render(<App url={path} />);
```

### Prerendering

The router also exposes a `ssgables` function which returns any route that doesn't have dynamic parameters in it to allow for easy prerendering.

```tsx
let paths = router.ssgables();
let template = /* index.html ... */;

for (const [route, path] of paths) {
	const rendered = await renderSsr(template, () => entry.default(route));
	console.log(`prerendered: ${route}`);
	let resolved = resolve("dist/static/" + path);
	await mkdir(dirname(resolved), { recursive: true });
	await writeFile(resolved, rendered);
}
```

# ssr.mdx

Source: https://github.com/mercuryworkshop/dreamlandjs/blob/rewrite/site/src/docs/extras/ssr.mdx

- Features
  - SSR
order: 31

dreamland's SSR implementation is based around DOM element construction order, so it is especially prone to hydration errors with differing logic on server vs client.
The server-side API is based around `domhandler`'s DOM with a custom internal DOM that implements the bare minimum needed for dreamland.
This internal DOM is exposed to components on the server-side when rendering to SSR.

## Integrating SSR with Vite

dreamland provides a Vite plugin to enable SSR on the dev server for easy setup:

1. Separate your entrypoint into a server, client, and common file.
   - The common file should export a function that handles instantiating your app and setting the router up
   - The server file should export a function that uses `render` from `dreamland/ssr/server` to render the common file's export into `domhandler` elements
   - The client file should use `hydrate` from `dreamland/ssr/client` to hydrate the common file's export. This is your new client entrypoint.
2. Add `<!--ssr-head-->` and `<!--ssr-body-->` to your html entrypoint, with `ssr-body` replacing the existing app root and `ssr-head` wherever you want to keep the SSR data.
3. Add the `devSsr` plugin to your vite.config.ts, configuring the server entrypoint with the `entry` key.
4. Confirm ssr is working and hydrating on the dev server.

You can use SSR in production builds as well by telling vite to build a SSR bundle with `--ssr` and the server entrypoint, importing your render function from that bundle, and using the `renderSsr` helper from `dreamland/vite` to render the page like the dev server does.

dreamland's router is strictly a layer above the dreamland core and SSR, so prerendering simply means telling your own code to route to a different path and saving that to a different file. You can check out this docs site's code (in the dreamland repo's site folder) for a working SSR + prerendering example.

---

# css.mdx

Source: https://github.com/mercuryworkshop/dreamlandjs/blob/rewrite/site/src/docs/features/css.mdx

- Core Features
  - Scoped CSS
order: 21

dreamland core comes with an optional built-in lightweight scoped component CSS solution.
It uses the browser's CSS parsing and a tiny CSS selector parser based on LeaVerou's [parsel](https://github.com/LeaVerou/parsel) to rewrite CSS for scoping.
Essentially, it adds `:where(.dlcss-tag)` to all selectors to make sure they only apply to elements within the component.
It also aliases `:scope` to `.dlcss-tag.dlc` to target the root of the component.
The scoping can be turned off by using `:global()`.

You can use it by assigning a call to the `css` template tag to the `style` property on a component:

```tsx
Card.style = css`
	:scope {
		background: var(--bg-3);
	}

	:global(*) > :scope {
		/* ... */
	}
`;
```

---

# stores.mdx

Source: https://github.com/mercuryworkshop/dreamlandjs/blob/rewrite/site/src/docs/features/stores.mdx

- Core Features
  - Stores
order: 20

If you need to store state persistently across loads, you can use dreamland's stores.
They work just like stateful objects, but automatically save and restore across loads.
dreamland core provides a `localStorage` backing and opt-in autosave or save-before-exit (`beforeunload`) i the core bundle.

You can make one with `createStore`:

```tsx
import { createStore } from "dreamland/util";

export let settings = createStore(
	{
		color: "#FFFFFF",
		fontSize: 16,
	},
	{ ident: "settings", backing: "localstorage", autosave: "auto" }
);
```

You can also provide an object containing optionally async `read` and `write` functions as a custom backing:

```tsx
import { createStore } from "dreamland/util";

let backing = {
	async read(ident: string): Promise<string | undefined> {
		// read from IDB or fetch externally...
	},
	async write(ident: string, value: string): Promise<void> {
		// write to IDB or post to server...
	},
};

export let settings = createStore(
	{
		color: "#FFFFFF",
		fontSize: 16,
	},
	{ ident: "settings", backing, autosave: "auto" }
);
```

You can manually save all stores at any time with the `saveAllStores` exported function.

---

# utilities.mdx

Source: https://github.com/mercuryworkshop/dreamlandjs/blob/rewrite/site/src/docs/features/utilities.mdx

- Core Features
  - Utilities
order: 22

dreamland core also provides some more miscallaneous sugar to make code look better.

## Reactive strings: usestr

You can use the `use` function as a template tag function to create string pointers:

```tsx
<div>
	<input placeholder={use`Hello, ${this.name}!`} />
</div>
```

This is useful for text or class strings which need to be recalculated.

## Delegates

Delegates make it easier to call functions on child components, which would instead require exposing a function on `this` and getting a reference to the component's state.
They are functions which have a `listen` function on them.

For example, you can create a delegate in the parent component and then pass it to the child component, which then calls `listen` on it:

```tsx
import { createDelegate } from "dreamland/core";

function Ripples(this: FC<{ create: Delegate<MouseEvent> }>) {
	this.cx.mount = () => {
		this.create.listen((e: MouseEvent) => {
			// create ripple...
		});
	};

	return <div />;
};

function Button(this: FC) {
	let ripple = createDelegate<MouseEvent>();

	return (
		<div on:pointerdown={ripple}>
			<Ripples create={ripple} />
		</div>
	);
};
```

---

# getting-started.mdx

Source: https://github.com/mercuryworkshop/dreamlandjs/blob/rewrite/site/src/docs/getting-started.mdx

- Getting Started
order: 0

dreamland is ESM-only and imports itself using node-style imports (ie `dreamland/router` imports `dreamland/core` to use the JSX factory).
This means you'll either need a bundler or an importmap to use it.
Additionally, dreamland exposes one global (the `use` function) with `Object.defineProperty` so it doesn't play nice with multiple versions in the dependency tree.
Sadly `use` can't be exported via ESM as the state system requires it to actually be a getter that returns a function.

dreamland targets the oldest browsers that support `:where()` (which is needed for dreamland's scoped CSS - similar to how Svelte needs it), which are **Chrome 88**, **Firefox 78**, and **Safari 14**. Transpilers can be used to run dreamland core on older versions, but scoped CSS will break.

## Pure JS

An importmap is required as dreamland imports itself internally. Here's an example importmap, assuming the dreamland package is in `dist`:

```html
<script type="importmap">
	{
		"imports": {
			"dreamland/core": "./dist/core.js",
			"dreamland/js-runtime": "./dist/js-runtime.js",
			"dreamland/router": "./dist/router.js"
		}
	}
</script>
```

Then you can use dreamland like normal JS with a bundler:

```html
<script type="module">
	import { css } from "dreamland/core";
	import { html } from "dreamland/js-runtime";

	function App() {
		this.count = 0;

		return html`
			<div>
				<h1>:3</h1>
				<button on:click=${() => this.count++}>
					Count: ${use(this.count)}
				</button>
			</div>
		`;
	};
	App.style = css`
		:scope {
			border: 4px dashed cornflowerblue;
			padding: 1em;
		}
	`;

	document.querySelector("#app").replaceWith(html`<${App} />`);
</script>
```

## TypeScript

Install dreamland (`pnpm i dreamland`) then add this to your tsconfig:

```json
{
	"compilerOptions": {
		"jsx": "react-jsx",
		"jsxImportSource": "dreamland"
	}
}
```

You can also use the old JSX transform (the `h(el, props, ...children)` one) by adding this to your tsconfig instead:

```json
{
	"compilerOptions": {
		"jsx": "react",
		"jsxFactory": "h",
		"jsxFragmentFactory": "Fragment"
	}
}
```

Note that you'll need to manually import `h` and `Fragment` from `dreamland/core` if you use this method.

## JS with bundlers (Vite, esbuild, etc)

If you're using vite, just add `jsxPlugin` from `dreamland/vite` to your vite config:

```js
import { jsxPlugin } from "dreamland/vite";
import { defineConfig } from "vite";

export default defineConfig({
	plugins: [jsxPlugin()],
});
```

This just sets the following vite esbuild config:

```js
{
	esbuild: {
		jsx: "automatic",
		jsxImportSource: "dreamland"
	}
}
```

dreamland provides a tagged template function for writing HTML in the `dreamland/js-runtime` export.

---

# state-system.mdx

Source: https://github.com/mercuryworkshop/dreamlandjs/blob/rewrite/site/src/docs/internals/state-system.mdx

- Internals
  - State System
order: 110

The state system's code is mostly in `src/core/state/` in the repository, split into separate files for the pointer code, the stateful object code, and the `use`/usestr code.

## The magic behind `use`

`createState` returns a `Proxy` that wraps the (target) object passed in.
It also registers a new `StateData` which has a listeners array, the target object, and a unique ID.
By default, the `Proxy` just forwards gets/sets to the target object and notifies listeners on the `StateData` when values are set.
This is where the `use` getter comes into play.

When `use` is called, JavaScript first calls the getter, which sets a "use trap" flag and returns the actual `use` function.
This "use trap" tells all stateful proxies to register a `PointerData` and return a new `Proxy` whenever a property is accessed.
The `Proxy` tracks any further accesses, effectively building a "path" of accesses from the state object to the target property.
It also turns into a `Symbol` ID corresponding to the `PointerData` when `Symbol.toPrimitive` is called on it.
Next, JavaScript parses the arguments list, triggering all the proxies and collecting the paths.
Finally, the `use` function is called which disables the "use trap", adds listeners to all stateful objects and pointers along the pointer's path, and returns a `Pointer<T>` linked to the `PointerData`.

---

# basic-html.mdx

Source: https://github.com/mercuryworkshop/dreamlandjs/blob/rewrite/site/src/docs/intro/basic-html.mdx

- Introduction
  - Basic HTML
order: 10

In dreamland, all components return a HTML element, unless you explicitly return something else like an array or other data.
The JSX factory always returns a HTML element.

```tsx
let button = <button class="a-button">click me!</button>;
document.body.appendChild(button);
```

This just created a button with the class `a-button`, and added it to the document.
This is the simplest possible way to use dreamland and also why it's so easy to migrate to or integrate it; it doesn't abstract away the DOM, instead only making it easier to use.

If you're coming from other frameworks like React, you might be used to using `className` instead of `class`. dreamland always uses `class` to match HTML.

## Syntax sugar for elements

For any DOM event, you can use the prop prefix `on` to add an event listener:

```tsx
<button on:click={() => alert("clicked!")}>click me!</button>
```

You can set properties on the element itself (like `innerHTML`) with the prop prefix `attr`:

```tsx
<div attr:innerHTML={markdownOutput} />
```

You can set inline styles regularly with a string, or you can pass an object with property names that `CSSStyleDeclaration`'s `setProperty` accepts (this includes CSS variables):

```tsx
let regularStyle = <div style="color: red; background: blue;" />;
let objectStyle = <div style={{ color: "red", background: "blue" }} />;
```

You can toggle on/off specific classes by using the prop prefix `class` (this becomes more useful when you pass a pointer to it):

```tsx
<div class="card container" class:active={true} />
```

---

# components.mdx

Source: https://github.com/mercuryworkshop/dreamlandjs/blob/rewrite/site/src/docs/intro/components.mdx

- Introduction
  - Components
order: 12

Components are self-contained pieces of HTML and JS that you can use elsewhere in your app.
The `this` value inside a component is automatically a `Stateful<T>`, so you can put state on `this` and have it automatically update.
Components return HTML elements when constructed, unless you manually return a Fragment or other data.

The `Component` type has 3 separate objects: `Props` which is all the JSX props passed to the componeont, `Private` which is private state, and `Public` which is public properties that aren't necessarily props. The `Stateful<T>` type for `this` in a component merges all 3 of these objects.

The first argument to a component is its `ComponentContext`, which is where you can access children passed to the component, add callbacks, access the root element once constructed, or get the raw Stateful object assigned to `this`.

```tsx
function Button(this: FC<{ title: string; children?: ComponentChild }>) {
	return (
		<div>
			{use(this.title)}
			<button>{this.children}</button>
		</div>
	);
};
```

## Lifecycle

`ComponentContext` has two main callbacks for initialization.
The most common one used is `mount`, which is run only on the client side once the component's HTML has been constructed (but not necessarily after it's been added to the DOM).
The other one is `init`, which runs in the same place as `mount` but is run on both the client and server side. `this.root`, the component's HTML root, is accessible in both `init` and `mount`. You realistically can't touch the DOM in `init` however, even though it's possible to do so, as the default server-side DOM is very minimal.

```tsx
function ChartView(this: FC) {
	this.cx.mount = () => {
		// mount the chart on the client once the canvas is constructed
		let chart = new Chart(this.root as HTMLCanvasElement, {
			/* ... */
		});

		// update the chart on data changes ...
	};

	return <canvas />;
};
```

If you need to easily access DOM elements in the component that aren't the root, you can pass a pointer to the special prop `this`:

```tsx
function ChartCard(this: FC<{}, {
	chart: HTMLCanvasElement
}>) {
	this.cx.mount = () => {
		// mount the chart on the client once the canvas is constructed
		let chart = new Chart(this.chart as HTMLCanvasElement, {
			/* ... */
		});

		// update the chart on data changes ...
	};

	return (
		<div>
			<h1>Chart</h1>
			<canvas this={use(this.chart)} />
		</div>
	);
};
```

## Dynamic props

`Pointer<T>`s passed as props are automatically "proxied" to the component's `this` value.
Effectively, any change to the pointer's value will change the property on the component's `this`, and any change to the property on the component's `this` will change the pointer's value.
This behavior is when the true power of the state system starts to show.

```tsx
function Input(this: FC<{ title: string; text: string }, { hint: string }>) {
	this.hint = "";

	use(this.text).listen((text) => {
		if (text.length < 3) this.hint = "too short!";
		if (text.length > 12) this.hint = "too long!";
	});

	return (
		<div>
			{this.title /* title won't change */}
			<input value={use(this.text)} />
			{use(this.hint)}
		</div>
	);
};

function SignUp(this: FC<{}, { user: string; password: string }>) {
	const submit = () => {
		// clear the inputs
		this.user = "";
		this.password = "";
	};

	return (
		<div>
			<h1>Sign Up</h1>
			<Input title="Username: " text={use(this.user)} />
			<Input title="Password: " text={use(this.password)} />
			<button on:click={submit}>Submit</button>
		</div>
	);
};
```

When the user types in the inputs, the changes ripple outwards from the `Input`'s `this.text`, then to the `SignUp`'s `this.user` or `this.passsword`.
Similarly, when the inputs are cleared in `SignUp`, the `Input`'s `this.text` will automatically get cleared and then clear the text in the input.

---

# reactivity.mdx

Source: https://github.com/mercuryworkshop/dreamlandjs/blob/rewrite/site/src/docs/intro/reactivity.mdx

- Introduction
  - Reactivity
order: 11

dreamland's state system is extremely simple, but it can often take some time to get comfortable. AI messes up a lot as well, since it's so used to React-style state.

Calling `use()` with a property from a stateful object will return a dynamic reference (the `Pointer<T>` class) that will listen to the property and automatically update/notify listeners as the data updates. Stateful objects can be created with `createState`:

```tsx
import { createState } from "dreamland/core";

let state = createState({
	count: 0,
});
(self as any).state = state;

document.body.appendChild(
	<div>
		<button on:click={() => state.count++}>click me!</button>
		<p>{use(state.count)}</p>
	</div>
);
```

Whenever `state.count` is updated, the specific nodes that depend on the value update to reflect the new value with minimal overhead.

This is done by listening to pointer value changes, like so:

```tsx
use(state.count).listen((val) => {
	console.log("new value! ", val);
	// update dom...
});
```

`state.count` has already updated to the new value once the listener is called, but the new value is provided as an argument for convenience.

## Transforming pointers

It's important to remember that `use` returns a pointer, not the actual value.
So, manipulating the value inside `use` will not work since the function is only executed once (see the state system internals page for more info):

```tsx
<div>
	<button on:click={() => state.count++}>click me!</button>
	{use(this.count % 2 == 0 ? "Even!" : "Odd") /* <-- won't work */}
</div>
```

To transform the actual value, use `Pointer`'s `map()` instead, like you would do with an array or some other light container:

```tsx
<div>
	<button on:click={() => state.count++}>click me!</button>
	{
		use(state.count).map((x) =>
			x % 2 == 0 ? "Even!" : "Odd"
		) /* <-- works! */
	}
</div>
```

This will work properly across updates, flipping between even and odd when the button is clicked.
Only the closure passed to `map` is rerun when `state.count` changes, not anything else.

If you want to allow setting the pointer's `value`, you can pass another closure to `map` to go in the opposite direction:

```tsx
let stringCount = use(state.count).map(
	(x) => "" + x,
	(x) => +x
);
stringCount.value = "5";
console.log(stringCount.value); // 5
```

If you don't want to allow specific changes, you can import the symbol `NO_CHANGE` from `dreamland/core` and return that from the reverse `map` instead.

## Advanced transformations

You can combine multiple pointers' changes into one pointer with `zip`.
If you want to combine multiple stateful values but haven't created pointers yet, you can pass multiple values to `use` as a shorthand instead.

```tsx
let counters = createState({
	one: 0,
	two: 1,
	three: 2,
});

let sum = use(counters.one)
	.zip(use(counters.two), use(counters.three))
	.map(([one, two, three]) => one + two + three);

let average = use(counters.one, counters.two, counters.three).map(
	([one, two, three]) => (one + two + three) / 3
);
```

To easily toggle between values (or lazily computed values) when you have a booleanish pointer, you can use `and` and `or`:

```tsx
let settings: Stateful<{
	darkMode: boolean,
	state: "one" | "two" | null,
}> = createState({
	darkMode: true,
	state: null,
});

let class = use(settings.darkMode).and("dark-mode").or("light-mode");
let state = use(settings.state).and((x) => "state-" + x).or("state-none");
```

If you have an arraylike value, you can map each element of the array instead of having to nest `map` closures by using `mapEach`:

```tsx
let cards: Pointer<string[]> = /* ... */;

let cardEls = cards.mapEach(x => <div>card: {x}</div>);
```

You can quickly negate a value using `not`:

```tsx
let enabled: Pointer<boolean> = /* ... */;
let disabled = enabled.not();
```

---

# migrating-from-v0-1-x.mdx

Source: https://github.com/mercuryworkshop/dreamlandjs/blob/rewrite/site/src/docs/migrating/migrating-from-v0-1-x.mdx

- Migrating
  - From v0.1.x
order: 100

## Component Syntax Revamp

Component syntax has changed drastically, using proper function syntax instead of anonymous functions assigned to variables:
- `Component` has two generic arguments: `Props` (stays the same as the old syntax) and `This` (maps to `Public & Private` in the old syntax)
- The new `FC` type is used as the `this` type on components, specifying `Props` and `This`.
- `cx` and `root` keys are no longer allowed to be used as props or internal state.
- `cx` has been removed as an argument. It is now on `this`.
- `root` and `children` have been moved from `cx` to `this`. `root` is still initialized after the initial component execution.
	- `children` has better types now, accurately representing that it will always be an array with elements being the type you specify in Props/This
- `DLElement` has been removed. Use `ComponentInstance` with a proper `Component` type instead.
- `ComponentContext` now takes a `Component` type to align with the other `Component*` helpers.

Here are some examples:
```tsx
// old
const App: Component = function () {
	return (
		<div>
			<NavBar />
			<div class="red">this text is red!</div>
		</div>
	);
};
App.style = css`
	:scope {
		height: 100vh;
	}
	.red {
		color: red;
	}
`;

// new
function App(this: FC) {
	return (
		<div>
			<NavBar />
			<div class="red">this text is red!</div>
		</div>
	);
};
App.style = css`
	:scope {
		height: 100vh;
	}
	.red {
		color: red;
	}
`;

// old
let ChartCard: Component<{}, { chart: HTMLCanvasElement }> = function (cx) {
	cx.mount = () => {
		// mount the chart on the client once the canvas is constructed
		let chart = new Chart(this.chart as HTMLCanvasElement, {
			/* ... */
		});

		// update the chart on data changes ...
	}

	return (
		<div>
			<h1>Chart</h1>
			<canvas this={use(this.chart)} />
		</div>
	);
};

// new
function ChartCard(this: FC<{}, {
	chart: HTMLCanvasElement
}>) {
	this.cx.mount = () => {
		// mount the chart on the client once the canvas is constructed
		let chart = new Chart(this.chart as HTMLCanvasElement, {
			/* ... */
		});

		// update the chart on data changes ...
	};

	return (
		<div>
			<h1>Chart</h1>
			<canvas this={use(this.chart)} />
		</div>
	);
};
```

## Rendering changes

`true`/`false` are no longer rendered as text, matching what React does visually. `null`/`undefined`/`boolean` are rendered as empty comments instead.

## Reactivity

`use(x).andThen(yes, no)` is now `use(x).and(yes).or(no)`

```tsx
// old
{
	use(this.mobile).andThen(<Mobile />, <Desktop />);
}

// new
{
	use(this.mobile).and(<Mobile />).or(<Desktop />);
}
```

## Router revamp

Layouts are no longer instantiated by the user.
Show targets that return functions are now cached instead of being reinstantiated every route invocation.
`Router.route` is no longer available, and now is automatically called for the initial navigation.

Async routes are now available!

### SSR/prerendering
Remove any manual `Router.route` calls with custom paths and replace them with the `initial` prop.
`initial` prop has the type `[path: string, origin: string]` and both must be specified. You can use a fake origin if needed.

## Stores
Stores have been moved to `dreamland/util`. There's also now a `deserializeState` and `serializeState` function for more powerful stores.

---

# migrating-from-v1.mdx

Source: https://github.com/mercuryworkshop/dreamlandjs/blob/rewrite/site/src/docs/migrating/migrating-from-v1.mdx

- Migrating
  - From v0.0.x
order: 110

## Imports

You now import from `dreamland/core`

```tsx
// old
import "dreamland/dev"; // or whatever

// new
import { css, createState, type FC } from "dreamland/core";
```

## Vite

`vite-plugin-dreamland` is replaced with `dreamland/vite`'s `jsxPlugin`, which is only used for non-TypeScript projects.

```ts
// old
import { defineConfig } from "vite";
import { dreamlandPlugin } from "vite-plugin-dreamland";

export default defineConfig({
	plugins: [dreamlandPlugin()],
});

// new
import { jsxPlugin } from "dreamland/vite";
import { defineConfig } from "vite";

export default defineConfig({
	plugins: [jsxPlugin()],
});
```

## Styles

For inline styles you now need to list the css name verbatim.

```tsx
// old
<div style={{ minWidth: "300px" }}>

// new
<div style={{ "min-width": "300px" }}>
```

For classes you now need to define them outside the component.

```tsx
// old
const App: Component = function () {
	this.css = `
      height: 100vh;
    `;

	const red = css`
		color: red;
	`;

	return (
		<div>
			<NavBar />
			<div class={red}>this text is red!</div>
		</div>
	);
};

// new
function App(this: FC) {
	return (
		<div>
			<NavBar />
			<div class="red">this text is red!</div>
		</div>
	);
};
App.style = css`
	:scope {
		height: 100vh;
	}
	.red {
		color: red;
	}
`;
```

## Reactivity

`useChange(x, () => {})` is now replaced with `use(x).listen(() => {})`

```tsx
// old
export const NavBar: Component<
	{},
	{
		pages: Record<string, { name: string; page: Component<any, any> }>;
		path: string;
	}
> = function () {
	this.path = new URL(document.URL).pathname;
	useChange(this.path, () => {
		let url = new URL(document.URL);
		url.pathname = this.path;
		if (window.location.toString() != url.toString()) {
			window.location.assign(url);
		}
	});

	return <div>Nav Bar</div>;
};

// new
export function NavBar(this: FC<{}, {
	pages: Record<string, { name: string; page: ComponentChild }>;
	path: string;
}>) {
	this.path = new URL(document.URL).pathname;
	use(this.path).listen((path) => {
		let url = new URL(document.URL);
		url.pathname = path;
		if (window.location.toString() != url.toString()) {
			window.location.assign(url);
		}
	});

	return <div>Nav Bar</div>;
};
```

`use(x, (x) => x)` with `use(x).map((x) => x)`

```tsx
// old
<div>
  {use(this.path, () => this.pages[this.path].page(this))}
</div>

// new
<div>
  {use(this.path).map((path) => this.pages[path].page)}
</div>
```

`$if(x, yes, no)` is now `use(x).and(yes, no).or()`

```tsx
// old
{
	$if(this.mobile, <Mobile />, <Desktop />);
}

// new
{
	use(this.mobile).and(<Mobile />).or(<Desktop />);
}
```

## `this` Object

Many items that were once accessed by `this.` are now accessed by `this.cx.` and JSX.Element is replaced with ComponentChild

```tsx
// old
export const Row: Component<{}, { children: JSX.Element }> = function () {
	this.mount = () => {
		(this.root.children[0] as HTMLDivElement).addEventListener(
			"mouseenter",
			() => {
				console.log("enter!");
			}
		);
	};
	return <div>{this.children}</div>;
};

// new
export function Row(this: FC<{ children: ComponentChild }, {}>) {
	this.cx.mount = () => {
		(this.children[0] as HTMLDivElement).addEventListener(
			"mouseenter",
			() => {
				console.log("enter!");
			}
		);
	};
	return <div>{this.children}</div>;
};
```
